CURB for Boston · October 2026

Built on
Boston's
curb data.

After our call on October 16, I built CURB for all of Boston on the City's data, and it went live the same day. Every swept curb is colored by its next sweep, with the Curb Lab's paid parking, resident permit, loading, accessible, time limit, snow emergency and no stopping curbs on top. Below are your questions from the call, what the map does with each one, and what we fixed in the data along the way.

From our October 16 call

Your questions, answered on the map.

Paraphrased from the call, in the order a resident would care about them.

On the map

“Residents open a curb map for two things: street sweeping and paid parking.”

Both lead the map. Every swept block is colored by its next sweep: green when it's clear, amber within 24 hours, red under 3 hours. Tap a side for the day and hours, the season, the City's holidays and the fine ($40, or $90 for overnight sweeping).

Paid parking shows as grey dots on 2,578 paid curbs, each with its rate and ParkBoston zone, and its time limit where one is posted.

On the map

“Is that curb data, or raw sign data?”

In Boston it's your curb data. The map reads the Curb Lab's CDS curb zones and their policies, all 54,185 zones, and sorts them into seven kinds of curb. Many signs are coded as exceptions, like no parking except resident permit. Reading those took resident permit curbs from 1,510 to 4,834, and accessible curbs from 56 to 1,568.

Sweeping comes from the Public Works schedule, which has no geometry, so each row is placed on the City's street segments (SAM) by street name, cross streets and odd or even side.

On the map

“Accessible parking is a great problem to solve, and nobody does it well.”

1,568 accessible curbs show in blue in the Loading & accessible layer, and a tap gives the rule. With the Curb Lab keeping the data current, an accessibility first view is a natural next map.

On the map

“Loading zones are everything from a planning point of view.”

2,660 loading zones by type: 1,220 bus, 634 commercial, 409 passenger, 169 valet, 136 short term parking and 92 rideshare. Yellow is commercial, white is passenger, rideshare and valet, orange is bus, green is short term.

On the map

“So with a resident permit you can park longer than two hours?”

That's how the resident permit layer reads: 4,834 permit curbs, either residents only or a time limit for everyone else. The block's sheet says which.

On the map

“Every stretch of curb has all its policies. Can a map show how the curb changes?”

Tap a curb side and its sheet lists every rule posted on that side, with its hours: 5,065 swept sides have at least one. Free time limits (1,294 curbs), snow emergency curbs (4,244) and no stopping or no parking curbs (15,061) each have their own layer too.

Alerts on the mapTicket times: not yet

“What do people want besides street cleaning? Do you send alerts?”

Sweep alerts work in Boston, on Boston time. They follow the City's holidays and the season, and an overnight sweep gets its alert around 9 PM the evening before. Calendar reminders work too, in Eastern time. On an iPhone, alerts come from the map added to the Home Screen; the CURB iPhone app is San Francisco only for now.

In San Francisco, two years of ticket times show when the sweeper really passes, so people know when they can park again. Boston doesn't publish ticket data, so that part waits for it.

Ready to use

“We'd love residents to help crowdsource what's really on the ground.”

Every block keeps CURB's report button, which sends the block and what's wrong with it. The cross checks further down make a first list to walk: on 227 block sides, the sign's weeks are the ones scheduled for the other side of the street.

How it's built

“Are you using static data?”

Yes. The map loads static files built from your API and the schedule, 2.1 MB of blocks and 4.4 MB of curb zones, so it never waits on a query. A rebuild picks up new data. Small area queries to the API took about 20 seconds each, while paging through it in bulk was fast.

It's also built phone first: every phone picture on this page is the live site, and the automated checks run on a phone screen, with a laptop pass for hovering and clicking.

Suggestions

“If the right API shape for public maps becomes obvious, let us know.”

From building this, in order of impact:

  • Renew the certificate on cds-curb-api.boston.gov, which expired on July 28. Meanwhile the map uses the Cloud Run address that curb-atlas uses.
  • Publish a nightly citywide export of curb zones with their policies resolved, as GeoJSON or vector tiles, so a map loads one file instead of hundreds of queries.
  • Publish the sweeping schedule with its route geometry, so nobody has to rebuild the join. 159 rows, 4%, still can't be placed on a street.
  • Serve a summary of the rules in force on each curb side, which is what a sheet shows. Ours covers the whole city in 30 KB compressed.
  • Mark zones that only have "unusable image" as unknown: 14,309 of the 54,185 zones, plus 11,426 with no policy.
Map fixes

Before and after.

Every block's line was checked against the streets the basemap is drawn from, and every street name against the City's street list. 7,140 of 7,410 lines sit within 4 m of their street. These are the changes, each one recorded with a small map on the fixes page.

Lines follow the streets

Zoomed out, the map drew each block as a straight line from end to end, which works for San Francisco's short, straight blocks. Boston's curve: 407 lines cut 10 m or more across their street, 41 of them over 50 m, up to 168 m. Every block now draws its real line at every zoom.

Pedestrian streets come off the parking map

10 blocks on the sweeping schedule are pedestrian streets: Downtown Crossing and Faneuil Hall Marketplace. The sweepers clean them, but there's no curb to park at, and where the Curb Lab read the signs, they say no stopping.

No street under the line

3 schedule lines have no street under them on the map: a stub past the end of Doone Ave, Eliot Pl and Haymarket Sq. They may be alleys the basemap is missing, so they're listed, ready to come back if the City says they're real.

Names spelled right

10 names on the schedule are wrong, on 22 blocks, Yawkey Way among them (Jersey St since 2018). 23 cross street names also get proper capitals, like Allen's Aly and McLellan St.

For the City

What the cross checks found.

Comparing the sweeping schedule, the street segments and the Curb Lab's signs block by block turned up a few things worth a look.

In the sweeping schedule

  • 10 street names are spelled differently from the City's street list, on 22 blocks. Yawkey Way is still Yawkey Way.
  • 10 blocks are pedestrian streets, in Downtown Crossing and Faneuil Hall Marketplace.
  • 3 lines have no street under them: a stub past Doone Ave, Eliot Pl and Haymarket Sq.
  • 159 of 3,758 rows can't be placed on a street segment from their names and cross streets.

Against the Curb Lab's signs

  • The signs show sweeping on 2,416 block sides: 2,129 of the schedule's, 15% of its sides, and 287 it doesn't sweep.
  • Of those 2,129, 1,771 agree on the day and hour, and 1,541 on the weeks too.
  • On 227 sides the sign's weeks are the other side of the street's: odd and even swapped in the schedule, in the sign reading, or in where the curb zone was drawn.
  • 14,309 of 54,185 zones have only "unusable image" policies, and 11,426 have none.
